open_points.subject: uploaded import file after owner-session expiry
open_points.text: A16 says “the upload of a session ended by its limits is dropped by the next holder,” while M11 says the file is kept “until ... the session ends; then it is dropped” and “Everything in it ends with the session.”
open_points.question: Does expiry drop the uploaded file immediately, or may its personal data remain in memory until another request takes the import lock?
options: Drop it synchronously when the session expires
Make it inaccessible at expiry but retain it until the next import-lock holder
Retain it until a bounded cleanup task runs
open_points.default_guess: Make it inaccessible at expiry and erase it when the next import-lock holder or restart performs cleanup.

open_points.subject: closure checks by import-lock holders
open_points.text: A16 says requests including “showing the mapping or the import's confirmation step, confirming, a sign-out” must “check the closure while holding” both locks, but rule 8 says only “uploading and confirming an import are refused” while the closure exists.
open_points.question: What must each mapping, confirmation-step, and sign-out request do when it finds the migration closure?
options: Refuse every import-related view but always complete sign-out
Refuse only upload and confirmation; allow stale mappings and confirmation steps
Clear import state and redirect import views to the closed result
open_points.default_guess: Refuse mapping and import-confirmation views as closed, while allowing sign-out to complete and clear the session.

open_points.subject: import file digest
open_points.text: A16 says “The mapping names the file by its digest” and binds confirmation to “the file's digest,” but no text defines the digest algorithm or the bytes over which it is computed.
open_points.question: Which digest algorithm and byte representation identify an uploaded import file?
options: SHA-256 of the exact uploaded bytes
A digest of a canonical parsed representation
A release-selected digest declared in the file contract
open_points.default_guess: Use SHA-256 of the exact uploaded bytes.

open_points.subject: owner-only configuration validation
open_points.text: A17 rule 1 permits “one service token for each service ... or, for an owner-only start, none of the four,” while rule 2 requires “every item of rule 1 present.”
open_points.question: How does the ordered presence check distinguish the valid no-token owner-only mode from an invalid partial set of service tokens?
options: Treat the four tokens as one all-or-none group
Require an explicit owner-only configuration value
Always require all four tokens
open_points.default_guess: Treat the four service-token variables as one all-or-none group and reject any partial group.

open_points.subject: REGISTRY_ configuration schema
open_points.text: A17 requires “no unknown item,” “every item ... present,” and “each well formed,” but gives item meanings rather than the accepted environment-variable names or the well-formedness rules for their values.
open_points.question: What are the exact accepted REGISTRY_ variable names, encodings, and well-formedness conditions for paths, credentials, tokens, and the backup key?
options: Define a fixed environment-variable schema in State 2
Leave names and value syntax to the release
Define names later but require the release to publish a machine-readable schema
open_points.default_guess: Define fixed names, UTF-8 string handling, path syntax, and secret decoding rules in the specification.

open_points.subject: secret strength
open_points.text: A17 says Registry checks only that a secret “is at least 32 bytes long” and “nothing else of how the owner made it,” but later justifies unlimited token attempts because “guessing 32 random bytes” is out of reach and concludes that a weak secret cannot be used.
open_points.question: Must service tokens and the backup key contain 32 bytes of generated entropy, or is any 32-byte value—including a predictable one—valid?
options: Require randomly generated 32-byte tokens and backup keys as an external invariant
Validate only length and remove the random-strength guarantee
Have Registry generate machine secrets
open_points.default_guess: Require the owner to generate service tokens and the backup key from at least 32 random bytes, while Registry validates only their encoded length.

open_points.subject: startup cleanup of temporary backup files
open_points.text: A17 says a probe that could not be removed is one “which the next start or run removes with the other temporary files,” but A17 defines no startup cleanup step; A18 removes temporary files only when a backup run occurs.
open_points.question: When and how must a later start remove a probe or other temporary backup file left by a failed start?
options: Clean all declared temporary-prefix files before the new writability probe
Clean only the known probe file during startup
Leave cleanup exclusively to the next backup run
open_points.default_guess: Before probing, startup should remove all files under the declared temporary prefix using the same bounded deletion rules as a backup run.

open_points.subject: backup encryption format
open_points.text: A18 says each backup “is encrypted with the backup key” and records metadata “readable without its key,” but defines no cipher, authenticated-encryption construction, nonce rule, key derivation, digest algorithm, or authentication of the unencrypted record.
open_points.question: What cryptographic format protects the backup ciphertext and binds its public metadata against tampering?
options: A versioned authenticated-encryption envelope covering both ciphertext and metadata
Encryption of the store with unauthenticated public metadata
A release-selected format documented outside these decisions
open_points.default_guess: Use a versioned authenticated-encryption envelope with a unique random nonce and authenticate all public metadata as associated data.

open_points.subject: backup keys after rotation
open_points.text: A18 says older backups remain encrypted with their former key and restoration uses “the key it was made with,” but configuration holds only the current backup key and no rule says where or how long former keys remain available.
open_points.question: How is every still-kept backup's former key retained and selected after a backup-key rotation?
options: The owner retains each former key until every backup using it is deleted
Registry re-encrypts all kept backups during rotation
Rotation is forbidden while backups made with the old key remain
open_points.default_guess: Require the owner to retain each former key, indexed by its recorded digest, until no kept backup uses it.

open_points.subject: temporary and kept backup namespace
open_points.text: A18 says Registry deletes “every file under the temporary prefix” and files “under the kept prefix,” with “two different prefixes the release declares,” but does not define the prefixes, name grammar, whether ‘under’ means direct directory entries or a recursive tree, or how symbolic links and non-regular files are handled.
open_points.question: Exactly which filesystem entries may Registry inspect, remove, rename, or delete in the backup location?
options: Only regular direct-child files matching fixed filename grammars; unlink symlinks without following them
Every recursively reachable entry whose name starts with the prefix
Any direct child whose name starts with the release-selected prefix
open_points.default_guess: Use fixed direct-child filename grammars, operate only on regular files, and never follow symbolic links.

open_points.subject: kept-name collision
open_points.text: A18 says “a backup whose kept name exists, or whose rename fails, is deleted,” without saying whether deletion targets the new temporary backup or the already-kept file occupying that name.
open_points.question: Which file is deleted when the destination kept name already exists?
options: Delete only the new temporary backup and preserve the existing kept backup
Delete the existing kept backup and retry the rename
Keep both under a collision suffix
open_points.default_guess: Preserve the existing kept backup and delete only the new temporary file.

open_points.subject: backup run result after cleanup errors
open_points.text: A18 says an unreadable or undeletable kept file “is reported, and it goes on with the next,” while rule 5 says “a step that fails ... the run fails”; it does not say whether a newly checked backup remains kept or whether the whole run is considered failed when later retention cleanup fails.
open_points.question: What is the run's result when backup creation succeeds but one or more retention deletions fail?
options: Keep the new backup but mark the run failed
Keep the new backup and mark the run partially successful
Delete the new backup and fail the run
open_points.default_guess: Keep the successfully checked backup, continue cleanup, and mark the run failed if any required deletion failed.

open_points.subject: erasure retention bound in backups
open_points.text: A18 claims erased values leave backups “at most 31 days after the erasure” while also allowing missed or failed runs to extend that period and stating “Registry bounds neither how long a run takes nor how old the newest kept backup may be.”
open_points.question: Is 31 days a hard maximum, a maximum only under an explicit successful-run timing assumption, or merely an expected schedule?
options: Make 31 days a hard enforced maximum
State it only as a bound when one run completes successfully each day within a bounded duration
Remove the maximum and describe deletion at the next successful cleanup after age exceeds 30 days
open_points.default_guess: Define deletion as occurring at the next successful cleanup after a backup exceeds 30 days and make no unconditional 31-day guarantee.

open_points.subject: backup check for an empty audit history
open_points.text: A18 requires the restored store's audit log to “end at the recorded sequence number,” while a new store can have no audit entries and the text does not define the recorded number or what ‘ends at’ means in that case.
open_points.question: What sequence value is recorded and how is the check evaluated when the audit log has never contained an entry?
options: Record 0 and require an empty log with the durable sequence counter at 0
Omit the sequence field until the first entry
Record a nullable sequence value
open_points.default_guess: Record 0 and require both an empty audit log and a durable next/last-sequence counter consistent with 0.
